background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: So thank you for letting me do this, but I'd love to, so a major magazine came out with the 10 best images of 2018 and there was a picture of you that was pretty great that they called the man in the middle. And so I'd love for you to kind of talk about what it was like to be the man in the middle in the capital.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, sometimes it's no fun because you're getting hit from all sides. And the picture describes in the nomination hearings when I asked for a one-week delay to have the federal investigation. And that was really the man in the middle at that point. The problem right now in the capital is that every incentive is for elected officials to, when a big issue comes along, whether it's debt and deficit or climate change or gun policy or nomination, anything like that, is to rush to your corner to get with your tribe and never indicate at all that you might be persuadable or that a hearing that you might be holding or an investigation that's going on might influence or inform your vote. Because if you indicate that, then you're the man in the middle and everybody is going after you. And it's not. It's not a comfortable position to be in. So everybody now just rushes to their corners. And that's part of the problem we have right now.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: So, I think we saw this in the capital, I think this was just about two years ago, when you guys were playing baseball. A bunch of congressmen playing baseball, and there was a shooting, a gunman shot, I think over 100 shots, a representative was wounded, along with maybe some others. Talk to us a little bit about that experience. You were on the field.

ground_truth: That was an awful, awful day, obviously. I was between home plate and first base when that first shot rang out. And we didn't know what it was until a few seconds later, a volley of shots rang out. And our third baseman said, there's a shooter, shooter. And I just remember the enduring image I'll have is turning toward the dugout and just running, the only cover I could find, and seeing the bullets pitch off the gravel in front of me. And I was thinking at that time, why us? How could somebody look at a bunch of middle-aged men playing baseball and see the enemy? And that's where our politics are right now. This man had been ginned up by talk radio and everything else. And he died on the scene. And they found on his body. A list of officials that he was going after. And it was a terrible scene. I had to rush out to the wounded representative and plug up the wound with my batting glove and then get his phone and call his wife so she wouldn't learn from television that her husband had been shot. So that's where our politics have gone. And we've got to get it back.

background.text: Yeah. I know that you and I both share a love for survival trips.

background.speaker: [target]

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: You've done some good ones, so I'd love, you go to some pretty extreme measures, so I'd love to hear you talk a little bit about the extreme measures you've gone to promote bipartisanship.

ground_truth: Well, I did my first survival trip 10 years ago. I love reading books about survival. Sailing adventures gone bad, that's my favorite genre. So I went alone for seven days and seven nights with no food or water, just marooned on an island in the Pacific Islands just to see if I could survive. I did, and a couple years later, I took our two youngest sons back to the islands, just a different island across the lagoon. And then when I got to the Senate, you know, the partisanship was so bad at that time, I thought, we'll go to extreme lengths. And so I got up with a Democratic senator from a southwestern state. And we decided to maroon ourselves on an island for a week and to prove to our colleagues that we could get along. So we went there with just basically a machete between us, no food, no water. The Discovery Channel came along. They wanted to film it. They did. This was not naked and afraid. Afraid, yes. But anyway, we did survive. It was a great experience. We got back and went on the circuit to talk about, you know, this bipartisanship. I remember we went on late-night shows, and then a TV host ran a clip of us, you know, Spear and Fist. And he said, [target] proved once and for all that Republicans and Democrats can get along if death is the only option. So for what it's worth, we've empirically proven it. But it was a great experience, and it's not out of my system yet. So stay tuned.
